# A complete guide to the languages at the 2022 World Cup

Author:

Kyle Carney

When the World Cup kicks off in just a few short weeks, it will be the 22nd running of the competition. As one of the premier sporting events in the world, it is truly a global event that brings together cultures from all over the world.  

As a melting pot of cultures, one of the most interesting aspects of the World Cup each year is language. This year, there will be 23 different official languages represented and how those languages are used on the field, in the stands and outside the stadiums is always fascinating.  

To help get you prepared for this year’s World Cup, we’ve put together a definitive list of all the different languages and cultures that will be present this year.

## Why the 2022 World Cup is different

Every World Cup brings something unique to the table. From the stadiums to the fans to the culture, the host country makes each World Cup a completely unique event. 

That being said, 2022 is truly a once-in-a-lifetime tournament. It is the first tournament to be hosted in an Arab country. It is also the first tournament to be held in the winter, unlike the traditional summer timeline for every other World Cup.  

How both of those firsts will ultimately be remembered will be determined in the weeks to come, but for now, they are worth mentioning as unique cultural elements that this World Cup will feature.

## What are the most common languages being spoken at the 2022 World Cup

Of the 23 total official languages represented at the World Cup, 7 of them are spoken in multiple countries. English is the most common, being listed as an official language of 9 countries competing in the World Cup. On top of being an official language, English is also a recognized language in nearly every country.

After English, French is the next most common language, followed by Spanish, Arabic, German, Dutch and Portuguese as the official languages of multiple countries in the World Cup.

## What are the least common languages being spoken at the 2022 World Cup

While there are definitely a lot of languages that are spoken in multiple countries, there are even more languages that are unique to a specific country. In fact, there are 16 languages at the World Cup that are only official in one country.

Of those 16, eight of them are regional languages that are generally not spoken outside of the country, including Amerindian, West Frisian, Limburgish, Welsh, Faroese, Greenlandic, Berber and Romash.

## What are the official languages for each country

Every country lists official languages. These are recognized as the languages spoken in that country by most of the population. These official languages generally do not include regional dialects used by small populations but are more focused on the overall population and what languages are spoken most often.

## Fun language facts to know before the 2022 World Cup

**Which player speaks the most languages at the World Cup?**

Romelu Lukaku is the winner when it comes to speaking the most languages, being conversational in 9 different languages. The Belgium forward grew up speaking French and Flemish, but also speaks English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch, Italian and Lingala.

![](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltacc1a01c4d280f24/bltcab138228c1e1426/63656544b294304eafc82f13/Romelu_Lukaku.png?auto=webp&format=pjpg&quality=80&)

**Which country has the most official languages?**

Switzerland is the most diverse in terms of the number of official languages, with 4 different languages listed. German, French, Italian and Romansh are all recognized as official languages on the country.

![](https://images.contentstack.io/v3/assets/bltacc1a01c4d280f24/blt1cd23a304075ae7b/636565c82d2a144cc904a0a7/Switzerland.png?auto=webp&format=pjpg&quality=80&)

So, there you have it; the complete guide to all the different languages that will be spoken in Qatar at the World Cup. Just imagine the poor referees who could be dealing with players speaking 4 or 5 different languages on the field.

The **2022 FIFA World Cup** was the 22nd [FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup "FIFA World Cup"), the quadrennial world championship for national [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") teams organised by [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA"). It took place in Qatar from 20 November to 18 December 2022, after the country was awarded the hosting rights in 2010. It was the first World Cup to be held in the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East "Middle East") and the [Arabian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula"), and the second in an Asian country after the [2002 tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup "2002 FIFA World Cup") in South Korea and Japan.[[A]](#cite_note-1)

This tournament was the last with 32 participating teams, before increasing to 48 for the [2026 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_World_Cup "2026 World Cup"). To avoid the extremes of [Qatar's hot climate in summers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Qatar#Climate "Geography of Qatar"),[[1]](#cite_note-auto5-2) the event was held in November and December, becoming the first to take place in the end of the year and outside the traditional months of May, June, and July.[[1]](#cite_note-auto5-2)[[2]](#cite_note-3) It was held over a reduced time frame of 29 days with 64 matches played in [eight venues](#Stadiums) across [five cities](#Cities). [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_national_football_team "Qatar national football team") entered the event—their first World Cup—automatically as the host's national team, alongside 31 teams determined by the [qualification process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification "2022 FIFA World Cup qualification").

[Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco_national_football_team "Morocco national football team") made history by becoming the first African nation to reach the semi-final of a World Cup, falling short 0–2 against [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_national_football_team "France national football team").[[3]](#cite_note-4) [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_football_team "Argentina national football team") were crowned the champions after winning [the final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup_final "2022 FIFA World Cup final") against the [title holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_FIFA_World_Cup_final "2018 FIFA World Cup final") [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_national_football_team "France national football team") 4–2 on penalties following a 3–3 draw after extra time. It was Argentina's third title and their first since [1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_FIFA_World_Cup "1986 FIFA World Cup"). Argentina were the first nation from outside of Europe to win the tournament since [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup "2002 FIFA World Cup"). French player [Kylian Mbappé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylian_Mbappé "Kylian Mbappé") became the first player to score a [hat-trick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hat-trick "Hat-trick") in a World Cup final since [Geoff Hurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Hurst "Geoff Hurst") in the [1966 final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_FIFA_World_Cup "1966 FIFA World Cup") and won the [Golden Boot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup_Golden_Boot "FIFA World Cup Golden Boot") as he scored the most goals (eight) during the tournament. Mbappé also became the first player to score in two consecutive finals since [Vavá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vavá "Vavá") of Brazil did the same in 1958 and 1962.

Argentine captain [Lionel Messi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Messi "Lionel Messi") was voted the tournament's best player, winning his second [Golden Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup_Golden_Ball "FIFA World Cup Golden Ball"). The tournament has been considered exceptionally poetic as the capstone of his career, with the win fulfilling for some commentators a previously unmet criterion to be regarded as the greatest player of all time.[[4]](#cite_note-NYT2022-5) Teammates [Emiliano Martínez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emiliano_Martínez "Emiliano Martínez") and [Enzo Fernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Fernández "Enzo Fernández") won the [Golden Glove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup_Golden_Glove "FIFA World Cup Golden Glove"), awarded to the tournament's best [goalkeeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) "Goalkeeper (association football)"), and the [Young Player Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup_Young_Player_Award "FIFA World Cup Young Player Award"), awarded to the tournament's best young player, respectively. With 172 goals, the tournament set a record for the highest number of goals scored in the 32-team format, with every participating team scoring at least one goal.

The choice to host the World Cup in Qatar [attracted significant criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup_controversies "2022 FIFA World Cup controversies"), with concerns raised over the country's [treatment of migrant workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_issues_involving_the_2022_FIFA_World_Cup "Human rights issues involving the 2022 FIFA World Cup"), [women](#LGBT_and_women's_rights), and [members of the LGBTQ+ community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_Qatar "LGBT rights in Qatar"), as well as Qatar's climate and [lack of a strong football culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup_controversies#Qatari_football_record "2022 FIFA World Cup controversies"). There were also allegations that Qatar used bribery to obtain hosting rights, as well as allegations of [wider FIFA corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_corruption_case "2015 FIFA corruption case").[[B]](#cite_note-14)

## Schedule

Unlike previous FIFA World Cups, which are typically played in June and July, because of [Qatar's intense summer heat and often fairly high humidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Qatar#Climate "Geography of Qatar"),[[1]](#cite_note-auto5-2)[[13]](#cite_note-auto6-15)[[14]](#cite_note-16) the 2022 World Cup was played in November and December.[[5]](#cite_note-Atlantic_2022-6)[[1]](#cite_note-auto5-2) As a result, the World Cup was unusually staged in the middle of the seasons of many domestic association football leagues, which started in late July or August, including all of the major European leagues, which had been obliged to incorporate extended breaks into their domestic schedules to accommodate the World Cup. Major European competitions had scheduled their respective competitions group matches to be played before the World Cup, to avoid playing group matches the following year.[[15]](#cite_note-17)

# The Languages of the World Cup Final

## Croatian and French: what connects these two languages?

[![Marco Neves](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/1*aGwgh4txGG7N7dzL8MiPJQ.jpeg)](/@marconeves?source=post_page---byline--7f8ecb385c9e-----------------------------------------)

[Marco Neves](/@marconeves?source=post_page---byline--7f8ecb385c9e-----------------------------------------)

5 min read

·

Jul 13, 2018

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1261/1*cd2yW_tAORpguXQyrpZOZw.png)

A few days ago, I promised myself I would write a piece about the languages of the World Cup final. I wasn’t worried: after all, it would most likely be a clash between the English and the French. I could speak about the old connection between the two languages, about the ancient history that led English to have swallowed so many French words that it sometimes seems like a Romance language. If Belgium won against France, it wouldn’t be difficult to find something to write about: linguistically speaking, Belgium is one of the most interesting countries of Europe…

Well, I got Croatia and France! What connects these two languages?

Before we go any further, let’s think for a moment about the third-place playoff. It’s the saddest game of the World Cup: the teams have already been knocked out, but they still have to play. In the end, the winner gets a bronze medal and tries to smile. In this case, and since we’re talking about languages, I just wanted to point out a curious fact: it seems that, on the pitch, both teams will speak in English. This is because the Belgian national team uses English as their usual language, since having to choose between French and Dutch could start a terrible row. So, they use the language of the island just over the sea — and that’s it. Nobody minds: almost all Belgian players play on that island anyway.

Moving on to the final. It will be one of the most watched spectacles in the world. The game that decides the World Champion of the most beloved sport on this planet. Even those who don’t like it won’t be able to avoid hearing about it.

Will Paris explode in celebration, allowing fans to forget their loss against Portugal two years ago? Or will the cup go to a country that, as an independent state, is younger than I am?

We’ll see. Before that, let’s start our journey through three words, in a game between Croatian and French:

## 1. ‘Le football’

The French language kicks off. Yes, we start with ‘football’. The word is written exactly like in English — the French did not change the spelling ever since football emerged from the islands.

Of course the pronunciation is French. I always think of *‘Allo‘Allo* whenever I hear a Frenchman say ‘le football’.

A curious fact. The sport may be of British origin, but FIFA is a French name: ‘Fédération internationale de football association’. ‘Football association’ is the French name for the original name of the sport in English: ‘association football’. And while the ball’s rolling, the word ‘association’ gave rise to the alternative name for the sport in English universities: ‘soccer’. Nowadays, this is the typical name for the sport in the USA, but its origin is very British…

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Let’s pass the ball to the beautiful Croatian language…

## 2. ‘Karta’

There, for ‘map’ you say ‘karta’. The two countries each have a very distinctive map: France is the hexagon many of us came to know while learning French culture at school. Croatia looks like Pacman eating Bosnia and Herzegovina:

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*8gb-_KuwA4J0h7dpyCJxcw.png)

It should be noted that ‘Croatia’ is ‘Hrvatska’ in Croatian. The name of the language is ‘hrvatski jezik’ (‘jezik’ means language).

Now we could be here for hours talking about the name of the language. Why? Because people can’t agree on whether Croatian and Serbian are two languages or two different names for the same language.

Let’s focus on the map. If we look closely, we see how Dubrovnik is there in a piece of Croatia separated from the rest of the country by a Bosnian corridor (in Neum). The Croatian coast is very narrow there: the country becomes narrower and narrower and hardly reaches ‘Crna Gora’, the Montenegrin name for ‘Montenegro’ (on this map, Montenegro wasn’t an independent country yet and there almost everyone would swear that the language was Serbian — or perhaps Serbian-Croatian).

Anyway, with so many countries having been created in recent decades and with such intertwined borders, it is not surprising to hear that people cannot agree where one language begins and another ends. So, we can count four languages (Bosnian, Croatian, Montenegrin and Serbian) or just one — it depends on your linguistic (or rather political) opinions. Even more curious: Serbian can be written using our Latin alphabet — or Cyrillic. It’s up to you! Not so in Croatia, where everyone uses the Latin alphabet…

## 3. ‘Gravata’ (necktie)

Well, Portugal is not in the final, but someone booted the ball and it landed in Lisbon. Why did I include a Portuguese word in this list? Here’s why: the origin of the Portuguese name for necktie (which is ‘gravata’) connects the two teams in the final.

The word ‘gravata’ comes from the French ‘cravate’. It’s hardly surprising: Portuguese has imported many words from the language of the Hexagon. What’s curious is to think that the French [got their ‘cravate’ directly from the Slavic ‘hrvat’](http://www.cnrtl.fr/definition/cravate)(let us remember ‘Hrvatska’) — or perhaps it was passed through German. One thing seems certain: in the history of the French language, there is a connection between ‘cravate’ (necktie)and ‘croate’ (Croat).

But what has the tie to do with the Croats? It seems that there was, under King Louis XIII, a [cavalry regiment](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A9giment_Royal-Cravates_cavalerie) formed by Croats at the service of the French monarch. Due to the whims of military fashion, a kind of short scarf was put around the necks of the Croats, similar to… a tie. So, in the language of the French, we moved from the ‘croates’ to the ‘cravates’ that these ‘croates’ had around their necks. The ‘cravates’ crossed the Pyrenees, set out on the road through Spain — where some of them settled as ‘corbatas’ — and landed in Portuguese in the form of ‘gravatas’.

If anyone asks why the Portuguese changed a ‘c’ into a ‘g’, notice that the sounds are remarkably similar. The tongue makes the same movements: to use the technical terms, we are talking about two occlusive velar consonants. The difference is in the vibration of the vocal cords, a detail that must have been missed by the Portuguese who heard ‘cravate’ for the first time.

And that’s it: these three words were enough to travel a bit through the two languages going head to head on Sunday — and we even talked about the vocal cords of the Portuguese…

Before finishing, I’d like to recall the first article published in this magazine, where I spoke about an old Romance language spoken in what today is the coast of Croatia: [“What do we lose when a tongue dies?”](/language-travels/what-do-we-lose-when-a-language-dies-5be184c0bc26)

And now let the best team win!

* What is the FIFA World Cup?

  The [FIFA World Cup](https://www.britannica.com/sports/World-Cup-football) is a quadrennial international men's football tournament contested by national teams. It is likely the most popular sporting event globally, drawing billions of television viewers.

  The first competition was held in 1930 and won by Uruguay. Except for interruptions during World War II, it has occurred every four years since. The final tournament involves 32 national teams. The [2022 FIFA World Cup](https://www.britannica.com/sports/2022-FIFA-World-Cup), hosted in Qatar, was won by Argentina, defeating France in the final.

It was the first World Cup to be held in the Middle East after FIFA (Fédération Internationale de Football Association) awarded Qatar the right to host the tournament in 2010.   The 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar was unique for several reasons:

  + It was the first World Cup held in the Middle East.
  + It was the first to be held in November-December to avoid Qatar's extreme summer heat, which disrupted the regular football season.
  + Qatar's national team was the only team new to the tournament.

**2022 FIFA World Cup**, international [football](https://www.britannica.com/sports/football-soccer) (soccer) tournament that took place in [Qatar](https://www.britannica.com/place/Qatar) from November 20 to December 18, 2022, and was contested by the men’s national teams of 32 countries. [Argentina](https://www.britannica.com/place/Argentina) won its third [World Cup](https://www.britannica.com/sports/World-Cup-football) victory in the tournament after defeating [France](https://www.britannica.com/place/France) in the final match.

The 2022 World Cup was the first to take place in the [Middle East](https://www.britannica.com/place/Middle-East) after the Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) awarded Qatar the right to host in 2010. Qatar’s national team was also the only one new to the tournament, although [Canada](https://www.britannica.com/place/Canada)’s team made its first appearance in nearly four decades and [Wales](https://www.britannica.com/place/Wales)’ team qualified for the first time since 1958. Only eight countries had won any of the 21 previous World Cup tournaments, and several of them, including Argentina, [Brazil](https://www.britannica.com/place/Brazil), [England](https://www.britannica.com/place/England), and France, entered the tournament among the favourites to win again. Preparation for the event proved to be a long and controversial road, however, from the launch of Qatar’s bid to host in 2009 to its final realization in 2022.

## Pitching the pitches: Qatar’s bid to host and its air-conditioned stadiums

[![Lusail Stadium: 2022 FIFA Men's World Cup in Qatar](https://cdn.britannica.com/53/239253-050-B8F1AB63/stadium-prior-to-the-FIFA-World-Cup-Qatar-2022-Lusail-City-Qatar.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/53/239253-050-B8F1AB63/stadium-prior-to-the-FIFA-World-Cup-Qatar-2022-Lusail-City-Qatar.jpg)

[Lusail Stadium: 2022 FIFA Men's World Cup in Qatar](https://cdn.britannica.com/53/239253-050-B8F1AB63/stadium-prior-to-the-FIFA-World-Cup-Qatar-2022-Lusail-City-Qatar.jpg)A general view outside Lusail Stadium prior to the 2022 FIFA World Cup semifinal match between Argentina and Croatia in Lusail City, Qatar, December 13, 2022.

When [Qatar](https://www.britannica.com/place/Qatar) launched its bid in 2009 to host the World Cup, it was in an overall strong position to make its case. The petroleum wealth of the [Persian Gulf](https://www.britannica.com/place/Persian-Gulf) region and its rapid, even luxurious, bloom left no doubt that Qatar (a leading producer of [natural gas](https://www.britannica.com/science/natural-gas)) could front the enormous expense of hosting the event. A successful presentation of the 2006 [Asian Games](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Asian-Games) in [Doha](https://www.britannica.com/place/Doha), its capital, further indicated that Qatar was up to the challenge.

 

Boosting Qatar’s appeal at the time was the image of the tiny country as a microcosm of global cooperation. It enjoyed [cordial and trusted relationships](https://www.britannica.com/place/Qatar/History#ref341564) that bridged both regional and global divides, in many cases serving as an intermediary between bitter rivals. The international success of its premier news broadcaster, [Al Jazeera](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Al-Jazeera), was perhaps the most visible example of Qatar’s global reach.

# Languages Represented at the Women’s Soccer World Cup 2023

[About](/language-schools/blog/about)

![Middlebury Language Schools students watch the world cup.](/language-schools/sites/default/files/styles/832x468/public/2023-05/Soccer%20Pic%201.jpg?fv=XUWu7Q_2&itok=a2IOSaFX) 

Language Schools students watch the Men’s World Cup in Summer 2018.

The FIFA Women’s Soccer World Cup is played every four years between women’s national teams. This summer it will be held July 20 to August 20, and will be hosted by Australia and New Zealand. The games will not be missed by students, faculty, and staff at the [Middlebury Language Schools](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools/).

The Women’s World Cup 2023 will have 32 teams participating, 29 qualified teams from around the globe, and three playoff tournament slot placeholders.

“Soccer, as the Americans call it, is the king of sports. Watching the beautiful game with the School of French is always a great time. My love for football most probably blinds me. Still, I always feel like these sports events have the ability to reunite students from all levels and all ages in such a special way”, said Connor Owens, Betty Ashbury Jones MA ’86 [School of French](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools/languages/french) Bilingual Assistant.

How many languages will be represented at the largest women’s soccer World Cup? Different teams will represent several languages and will be featured for viewers all around the world.

![Students in the School of French cheer on the French soccer team.](/language-schools/sites/default/files/styles/1136x639/public/2023-05/Soccer2.jpg?fv=bBbNaqX7&itok=Nv-WlL0U)

## **Women’s World Cup Soccer 2023 Teams**

20 countries participated in the previous round of qualification in 2019, which resulted in the 32 nations qualifying for the FIFA Women’s World Cup in 2023. Now, it is official that all qualified teams will take part in the upcoming Women’s Soccer World Cup.

Here is a list of all the teams that have qualified for the World Cup:

## **Languages Represented at the Women’s Soccer World Cup 2023**

Since this is a global cup featuring different teams worldwide, the Women’s Soccer World Cup 2023 will have languages from 32 different nations. Knowing the languages, or perhaps [learning a new language](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools/languages), will make watching the biggest women’s soccer tournament even more enjoyable.

### **English**

[English](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools//languages/english) will be the main language that is going to be featured throughout the Women’s Soccer World Cup 2023. Several teams participating in the tournament are also from countries that use English as the official language. These participating countries include the United States, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and Zambia.

### **Spanish**

[Spanish](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools//languages/spanish) is another language that will be represented in the women’s soccer world cup. This is the official language of Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama, and Spain; it is a language that the vast majority of people from the said countries understand and use as their first language.

### **Portuguese**

[Portuguese](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools//languages/portuguese) is the primary language of most people in Portugal and Brazil. Both are participating in the competition, and Portuguese will undoubtedly be featured because it is among the most popular languages among the most ardent soccer fans.

### **Irish**

Irish is a recognized language in the European Union and is the first official language of the Republic of Ireland. The Irish language will be represented by the national team of the Republic of Ireland, who will participate in the competition.

### **Afrikaans**

Given Africa’s size, Afrikaans holds the same status as English as an official language in South Africa. The Women’s Soccer World Cup 2023 will feature the Afrikaans language so that African people and others who speak it can follow their team.

### **Swedish**

Swedish language, or Swedish Svenska, is the official language of Sweden. The Swedish language will be represented by the Sweden team that is participating in the Women’s Soccer World Cup 2023

### **French**

[French](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools//languages/french) is another popular language that will be represented at the Women’s Soccer World Cup 2023. Its biggest representative will, of course, be France. Some nations playing in the competition will also represent French, even if it is not their primary language, since it is one of their most widely spoken languages. These countries include Canada, Switzerland, South Africa, Italy, and England.

### **Mandarin**

[Mandarin](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools//languages/chinese) is the official language of China that will be represented by the Chinese team at the 2023 Women’s Soccer World Cup. Due to the large number of people in China who are soccer fans, it is only fair that the language will be represented and the event will also be aired in Mandarin.

### **Korean**

The [Korean](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools//languages/korean) language will be represented by the team from the Korean Republic. Korean is the official language of both North Korea and South Korea and is spoken by around 77 million people worldwide. The Korean Republic team will bring its unique language and culture to the tournament, adding to the already diverse mix of languages and cultures the competing teams represent.

### **Japanese**

[Japanese](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools/languages/japanese) is another language represented at the 2023 Women’s Soccer World Cup, as Japan has qualified for the tournament and will be one of the competing teams. Japanese is the official language of Japan and is spoken by over 125 million people worldwide. Japanese players, coaches, and officials will likely communicate in their native language during the tournament, adding to the linguistic diversity of the event.

### **Vietnamese**

The Vietnamese team will proudly represent the Vietnamese language at the Women’s Soccer World Cup 2023. As one of the participating countries, Vietnam will showcase its sporting prowess and its unique cultural identity and language.

### **Tagalog**

Tagalog (Filipino) and English are the official language of the Philippines. They are one of the teams competing in the tournament with a large base of soccer supporters, not just in the Philippines but elsewhere in the world where the Tagalog language is widely spoken.

### **Danish**

The Danish team will represent Denmark’s only official language — Danish. Their team will represent the Danish language for the fans to support and cheer on their team.

### **German**

Germany’s team will represent [German](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools//languages/german), the official language of Germany. German is also spoken in Switzerland; broadcasting German would benefit fans rooting for their teams.

### **Norwegian**

Norwegian is only one of the official languages of Norway. However, the Norwegian language has been considered by many as the primary language. The national team of Norway will represent the language.

![Three spanish language school students playing soccer with referee in background.](/language-schools/sites/default/files/styles/1136x639/public/2019-10/5-soccer-activities-gallery.jpg?fv=iGyzMvUD&itok=QD5ODTrp) 

*Playing soccer at Middlebury Language Schools*

## **Watching the World Cup with the Language Pledge®**

It is incredible how a single competition may represent so many different languages from various countries. How much more incredible is it if you learn the language and watch with your classmates during language school while only speaking your target language?

Owens said, “For the rest of my life, I will always remember [screaming in Dana Auditorium](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=768871949903785&ref=sharing) when France won the men’s world cup in 2018. The place was absolutely packed, and there were even a few Spanish school students who managed to sneak in, which was actually kind of great. The same thing happened when the USA won the Women’s World Cup the following year. I will also always remember crying when England lost the final of the Euro 2021. Again, the room was packed, and students were learning loads of sports vocabulary.”

[Middlebury Language Schools](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools/) is a top-ranked language school that enrolls over 1500 students in in Middlebury and Bennington, Vermont. Middlebury also has a 7-week English Language School in Monterey, California.

Our summer [immersion programs](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools/how-it-works/programs/immersion) in 13 languages range from one to eight weeks and are designed for beginners to advanced language learners. We also offer [Graduate Programs](https://www.middlebury.edu/language-schools/how-it-works/programs/graduate) in 10 languages, which can be completed over four summers in Vermont or one summer and an academic year abroad or online, depending on the language you want to learn.
